name: Black seed oil hair

lead: Black seed oil comes from Nigella sativa seeds and has a long folk-medicine history. Some communities use it, on the scalp or orally, for thicker hair and less loss.

Its main active compound, thymoquinone, is the usual reason cited, and has been studied mostly for anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects in the lab. The sources reviewed contain no hair studies; research on it covers other conditions.

paras: It is applied to the scalp as an oil or taken orally as a supplement, as a regular routine over months.
The FDA classifies the plant as generally recognized as safe as a spice or flavoring; this concerns food use. The sources reviewed did not cover safety of the oil on the scalp.

chain: Nigella oil on scalp or oral
angle.text: Black seed oil is promoted in some communities for thicker hair and less loss, applied to the scalp or taken orally. Its thymoquinone content is the usual reason cited, with an anti-inflammatory action the proposed route. Research on it has centred on other conditions, and none was found on hair.

lead: Black seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Nigella sativa, also called black cumin. Its best-known constituent is thymoquinone [1][2]. It is promoted in some communities for hair thickness and loss, often applied to the scalp or taken orally.

The sources reviewed contain no hair studies of black seed oil. Published research on it concerns other conditions, and Wikipedia notes insufficient high-quality clinical evidence that the seeds or oil treat human diseases [1].
infobox: Folk medicine in Africa and Asia

paras: Seeds have been found at ancient Egyptian sites, including Tutankhamun's tomb, and Avicenna's Canon of Medicine describes their medicinal use [1]. A 2008 review discusses the therapeutic potential of black cumin [2].

No studies found for hair. Registered human trials of black seed oil examine other conditions, such as osteoarthritis [3], asthma [4], type 2 diabetes [5] and hypertension [6]. Laboratory research on thymoquinone has focused largely on cancer cells [7].
